extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, IP practitioners, students and general readers seeking an overview of patent application practice
extracted.subtask_description: An overview of the requirements, types, procedural steps, and legal standards relevant to preparing, filing, prosecuting, and maintaining patent applications (national, regional, and PCT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable a technical solution must be (1) new, (2) involve an inventive step, and (3) be industrially applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core substantive standard applied by patent offices; novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness), and industrial applicability are assessed against prior art and the claimed subject-matter. The page treats these three elements as the essential test for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility models protect inventions which are new and industrially applicable; they do not need an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility models are a distinct protection in some jurisdictions with different substantive and term rules (example: shorter, often non-renewable terms such as 7 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard (non-provisional) application contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard patent application is a patent application containing all of the necessary parts (e.g. a written description of the invention and claims) that are required for the grant of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contents usually include description, claims, drawings (where necessary), abstract and title; whether a given document constitutes a complete application depends on the office's formal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional application requirements and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Provisional patent applications (where available, e.g., USPTO) can establish a priority date only if the disclosure is enabling; claims are not required though advised; they expire (typically one year), are not published, and do not by themselves give enforceable rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A provisional may be incorporated into a later full (non-provisional) application. Non‑provisional applications may add further information; priority/novelty analysis may result in multiple priority dates for material first disclosed in the provisional vs. later filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation and continuation-in-part applications
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain offices a patent application can be filed as a continuation of a previous application (including continuation-in-part), enabling inclusion of material from a previous application when further refinement is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuation practice allows applicants to pursue additional claim sets or refinements after an earlier filing; different types (continuation, continuation-in-part) have different rules about added subject matter and priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional application constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: A divisional patent application is one which has been 'divided' from an existing application; it can only contain subject matter in the application from which it is divided (its parent) and retains the filing and priority date of the parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisional applications are used to pursue additional inventions when a unity-of-invention objection is issued; parent/child subject matter limits are strict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent specification required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent specification generally contains background and overview of the invention, a description of the invention and embodiments, claims, figures (where helpful), and an abstract and title; may include gene sequences or computer code depending on subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offices set formal rules on structure, paper size, font, layout, section ordering and headings. Because descriptions cannot generally be modified once filed (with narrow exceptions), careful preparation is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define scope and claim drafting constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims of a patent specification define the scope of protection; they describe the invention in a specific legal style, setting out essential features to clearly define what would infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims often include independent (broad) and dependent (narrower) claims and are frequently amended during prosecution. In the U.S., claims can be amended after grant but cannot be broadened beyond what was originally disclosed; claim broadening after grant is restricted (no broadening more than two years after issue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date effects and advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: The filing date of an application sets a cutoff date after which public disclosures cannot form prior art; in most jurisdictions the right to a patent belongs to the first person to file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is generally beneficial to file as soon as possible. To obtain a filing date, filed documents must comply with the patent office's regulations (some offices require fewer elements to secure a filing date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal requirements for obtaining a filing date under the PLT
rubrics_metrics.description: For PLT Contracting Parties, an office must accord a filing date upon compliance with three simple formal requirements: (1) an indication that the elements received are intended to be an application for a patent for an invention; (2) indications allowing identification/contact of the applicant; (3) a part which appears to be a description of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Contracting Party cannot require claims or a filing fee as part of the filing date requirement. These are absolute minimums for a filing date under the Patent Law Treaty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority claim (Paris Convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application may claim priority from one or more previously filed applications to take advantage of the earlier filing date (in respect of information contained in those earlier applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claiming priority reduces prior art exposure and allows delaying filings in other countries (commonly up to one year). Rules follow the Paris Convention and should not be confused with PCT procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security review and foreign filing licences
rubrics_metrics.description: Many national offices require security clearance prior to filing abroad; applications are reviewed for national security sensitive material and secrecy orders may be imposed preventing publication and/or foreign filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filing outside the inventor's country of residence is desired, a foreign filing licence may be required. Some offices (e.g., USPTO) may grant an automatic license after a set period if no secrecy order is issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing and effect as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications are generally published 18 months after the earliest priority date; publication makes the application publicly available and it then forms full prior art for other applications worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to publication the application is confidential to the office; after publication, communications between applicant/agent and the office commonly become public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and rules for 'patent pending' marking
rubrics_metrics.description: The expression 'patent pending' warns that an invention is the subject of a patent application; marking rules and benefits vary among patent offices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally permissible to mark products patent pending if there is in fact a patent application for an invention implemented in the product; local rules differ on consequences and enforcement benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject-matter exclusions vary by jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent laws restrict areas in which patents may be granted (exclusions from patentability). The scope differs by jurisdiction (e.g., Europe often excludes software and methods of performing mental acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject-matter eligibility is contentious and jurisdiction‑specific; applicants should check local law and case practice for excluded categories and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and search report purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: After filing a search is carried out to reveal prior art relevant to the claimed subject‑matter; a search report is generally published with the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search reports help applicants decide whether to pursue prosecution or abandon, and inform the public/competitors about the likely scope of protection. In some jurisdictions search and examination are combined and no separate search report is issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination and office actions (iterative prosecution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination ensures compliance with patent law requirements; it is generally iterative via office actions where the office raises objections and the applicant responds with arguments or amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses may be accepted or rejected, leading to further rounds. Many offices offer prioritized examination programs (targeting domains or small firms), which can speed up prosecution and affect outcomes (e.g., Track One statistics cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue/grant formalities and regional validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an application complies with office requirements, a patent is granted upon payment of further fees; in some regional systems validating the patent requires translations into official languages of states where protection is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue date effectively terminates prosecution for that application and establishes the date upon which infringement actions may be charged; patent term calculations may vary by filing/issue date and jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance fees and patent term retention
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jurisdictions require periodic payment of maintenance (renewal) fees to retain validity during the patent term; failure to timely pay fees results in loss of protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants/patentees must monitor fee schedules and grace periods to avoid lapse; restoration procedures vary by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑grant challenges and re-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: The validity of an issued patent may be subject to post-issue challenges (oppositions, re-examinations, etc.) that can cause the office to re-examine the application/patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various national and regional procedures exist to challenge patents after grant; outcomes can affect enforceability and term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights conferred by a patent and statutory exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent confers the right to prevent third parties from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing (product patents) or using the claimed process and products obtained directly by it (process patents) without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent confers exclusionary rights, not a positive right to exploit. Many laws provide exceptions (private non-commercial acts, experimental/scientific research, regulatory approval use) and mechanisms like compulsory licences or government use in the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of invention is a legal requirement that may be objected to by an examiner; lack of unity can trigger divisional filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a unity objection is issued the applicant may divide the application into divisional applications to protect further inventions disclosed in the parent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency (enabling) of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure in an application must be enabling (sufficient) so that the skilled person can carry out the invention; insufficiency can jeopardize priority and patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisional applications used to establish priority must also be enabling for the material they are relied upon for; sufficiency is a substantive legal requirement in many jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings and figure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings may be included to illustrate the invention; generally drawings must be in black and white and without colorings unless otherwise allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether drawings are required depends on whether they are necessary for understanding the invention; offices have formal requirements for presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Most patent offices require an abstract which provides a summary of the invention to aid searching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International/PCT and regional (e.g., EPO) applications must include an abstract as part of the required elements; abstract content and length are subject to office rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required elements of a PCT (international) application
rubrics_metrics.description: An international (PCT) application must contain the following elements: request, description, claim or claims, one or more drawings (where necessary), and abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO coordinates centralised filing formalities, international searches by ISAs, publication, and preliminary examinations by IPEAs. The PCT preserves national phase options and delays national prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office-specific formalities for specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Each patent office has rules relating to the form of the specification, defining paper size, font, layout, section ordering and headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must follow the target office's formal requirements to avoid deficiencies; some formal defects can be corrected without losing the filing date, others may affect the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date and inability to add subject matter afterwards
rubrics_metrics.description: Since no subject matter can be added to an application after the filing date (subject to narrow exceptions), it is important that an application disclose all material relevant to the invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to include material at filing may preclude later claiming of that matter; strategic decisions (e.g., provisional filings vs full) affect what can later be relied upon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects and statistics of prioritized examination programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Many offices have programs of prioritized examination targeted at specific domains or small firms; post-program studies show small firms are more likely to apply and Track One patents were more likely to be cited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may consider accelerated programs for faster prosecution; statistical effects on grant likelihood and citation may inform strategy.
